title: When the Interior Breaks
premise: August Ishikawa, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost the ability to taste after a betrayal they refuse to name, has spent a decade cultivating professional invisibility. When a box of undelivered letters surfaces behind a wardrobe in their late mother's house, August discovers their mother had been secretly corresponding with the father August believed abandoned them—and that the letters reveal a family history built on a lie August themselves helped protect. As August traces the letters' recipients, including a dying man who claims to be their half-brother, they must choose between preserving the loyal silence that made them powerful and telling a truth that could destroy what remains of their family. In the end, August publishes one final review—an honest account of a meal cooked from their father's recipes—tasting it fully for the first time, and forgives both the stranger in the photographs and themselves.
about_author: Cyrus Oyelaran is a former line cook turned novelist who writes about appetite, inheritance, and the lies families keep warm. He lives between Lagos and Lisbon, where he claims to still taste everything twice.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: August's POV. We meet August at the height of their career, writing devastating reviews of meals they cannot taste, performing pleasure with surgical precision. A young chef publicly begs for mercy at a launch party; August deploys the smile. Emotional beat: hollow mastery—the reader sees the armor before August admits it exists.

chapters.title: Salt Without Signal
chapters.summary: August's POV, flashback woven into present. The origin of the loss: the night ten years ago when August's mother, Marguerite, asked them to swear never to contact their father, and August agreed over a final home-cooked meal that went flavorless mid-bite. Emotional beat: grief disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: August's POV. Clearing Marguerite's house after her death, August pries loose a warped back panel and finds a shoebox: forty-one letters, all addressed but undelivered, in two hands—Marguerite's and someone else's. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past refuses its assigned shape.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: August's POV, intercut with letter text. The earliest letters are tender, coded—two people writing around a shared secret. August recognizes their father Daniel's handwriting and realizes Marguerite wrote back for years after the supposed abandonment. Emotional beat: betrayal reassembling itself into something more complicated.

chapters.title: The Editor's Patience
chapters.summary: August's POV with secondary character Vivienne, August's editor, who senses the critic is unraveling and offers a sabbatical shaped like a threat. August deflects with charm; Vivienne names it plainly: 'You review food like a coroner.' Emotional beat: being seen against one's will.

chapters.title: Undisclosed Organization
chapters.summary: August's POV. Following an address on an envelope, August finds a shuttered restaurant, The Interior, where Daniel was once head chef—and learns it closed the same month August swore the oath. A former waiter mistakes August for 'the child in the photographs.' Emotional beat: the past has witnesses.

chapters.title: Half of Everything
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: August and Tomas, a hospice nurse in his fifties who has been waiting decades for a call. Tomas reveals he is Daniel's son—August's half-brother—and that Daniel is dying and asking for August by name. Emotional beat: reluctant kinship, suspicion braided with longing.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Protected
chapters.summary: August's POV. Reading the middle letters, August reconstructs the truth: Daniel didn't abandon them—he discovered Marguerite was embezzling from The Interior's investors to fund August's elite schooling, and chose exile over exposure. His silence was his loyalty; hers was her corruption. Emotional beat: the ground tilting.

chapters.title: The Review That Ruined a Man
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas recounts how August's first great review—a evisceration of The Interior—was the final blow that closed the restaurant and broke Daniel's health. August, reading Tomas's account, realizes their career was built on destroying their own father, guided by Marguerite's quiet suggestion of the target. Emotional beat: complicity dawning.

chapters.title: Duty Calls Collect
chapters.summary: August's POV. The newspaper offers August their dream assignment: a legacy profile series, prestige and power consolidated. Accepting means staying silent forever; the deadline lands the same week as Daniel's. August accepts, then immediately regrets it. Emotional beat: ambition as anesthesia, wearing off.

chapters.title: Vivienne's Version
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She confesses she knew Daniel—she was the investor Marguerite defrauded, and she hired August years ago partly out of guilt, partly surveillance. She urges August to publish the truth and destroy them both. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as debt; truth offered as revenge.

chapters.title: Taste Memory
chapters.summary: August's POV. Cooking alone at midnight from a recipe card in Daniel's letters, August experiences a flicker—half a second of actual taste, gone instantly. They realize the loss was never neurological; it was the body refusing to enjoy what the conscience couldn't digest. Emotional beat: fragile hope.

chapters.title: The Hospital Corridor
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: August and Tomas outside Daniel's room. August freezes at the door, rehearsing the smile; Tomas, furious, tells them Daniel has waited thirty years and doesn't need the performance. August walks away without going in. Emotional beat: cowardice in real time, unforgivable and human.

chapters.title: Power's Quiet Kitchen
chapters.summary: August's POV. At a gala celebrating the new contract, August watches a powerful editor destroy a young writer's career with a compliment, and recognizes their own technique magnified. Power, August sees, is just inherited fear wearing better clothes. Emotional beat: revulsion at one's own reflection.

chapters.title: The Forty-Second Letter
chapters.summary: August's POV. Among the papers is an unmailed letter in Marguerite's hand, written in her final weeks: a confession meant for August, admitting everything and asking forgiveness she never requested aloud while alive. It ends: 'Tell your father I kept his letters because they were the only honest thing in the house.' Emotional beat: posthumous intimacy, too late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: Breaking the Oath
chapters.summary: August's POV. August mails every letter—to Daniel, to the old investors, to Vivienne—then drives through the night to the hospital. In the corridor they pass Tomas carrying a small box of Daniel's belongings. Emotional beat: dread and release arriving together.

chapters.title: Broth
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV, lucid for one hour. Father and child finally speak—not in apology but in inventory: what each kept silent and why. Daniel asks only that August eat something he can no longer cook, and describes the broth of August's childhood in such detail that August weeps. Emotional beat: forgiveness as recognition, not absolution.

chapters.title: The Final Review
chapters.summary: August's POV. In The Interior's gutted kitchen, August cooks Daniel's broth with Tomas beside them, and tastes it—fully, overwhelmingly, painfully alive. They write the review not of the dish but of the thirty-year silence, naming Marguerite, Daniel, and themselves. Emotional beat: catharsis; the critic becomes a witness.

chapters.title: Publication Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs: Vivienne reading at her desk, Tomas at the hospital, strangers in cafés. The essay detonates—some call it a confession, some a masterpiece, some a betrayal of the profession. August reads none of the coverage. Emotional beat: the strange lightness of having nothing left to hide.

chapters.title: What the Industry Decides
chapters.summary: August's POV before a tribunal of editors. Offered a choice: recant the personal turn or resign. August resigns, handing Vivienne the contract torn in half—an act she accepts with something like relief. Emotional beat: power relinquished voluntarily for the first time in August's life.

chapters.title: The Interior, Reopened
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, months later. He and August reopen The Interior as a small supper club serving Daniel's recovered recipes, Daniel attending in a wheelchair as 'consultant.' August waits tables instead of judging. Emotional beat: love rebuilt as labor, duty transmuted into devotion.

chapters.title: Everything Tastes Like This
chapters.summary: August's POV, closing frame. At the wardrobes of the finished house, now sold, August leaves one letter behind in the panel—for whatever stranger clears it next—a note explaining that the truth behind walls keeps poorly, but keeps. Over a simple meal, August tastes every layer. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace; the interior breaks open and lets the light feed everyone.
